entries.english_text:
1805—Hakim ibn Hizam [1]

[1] Asad al-Ghaba, biog. no. (1234); al-Istiʿab, biog. no. (553); Musnad Ahmad, 4/401, 403; Nasab Quraysh, 231; Tabaqat Khalifa, biog. nos. 70, 473; Tarikh al-Bukhari, 3/11; al-Maʿarif, 311; al-Jarh wa-al-Taʿdil, 3/202; al-Mustadrak, 3/482–485; Jamharat Ansab al-ʿArab, 121; al-Jamʿ Bayt Rijal al-Sahihayn, 1/105; Tarikh Ibn ʿAsakir, 5/123; Tahdhib al-Asmaʾ wa-al-Lughat, q. 1, h. 1, 166; Tahdhib al-Kamal, 321; Tarikh al-Islam, 2/277; al-ʿIbar, 1/60; Tadhhib al-Tahdhib, 1/169; Mirʾat al-Janan, 1/127.

He was Hakim ibn Hizam ibn Khuwaylid ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzza ibn Qusayy, al-Asadi, the son of the brother of Khadija, the wife of the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace).

His mother’s name was Safiyya; it is also said to have been Fakhita; and it is also said that she was Zaynab bint Zuhayr ibn al-Harith ibn Asad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzza. His kunya was Abu Khalid. Traditions from him are found in the Six Books.

His son Hizam, ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Harith ibn Nawfal, Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib, Musa ibn Talha, ʿUrwa, and others related from him.

Musa ibn ʿUqba said, on the authority of Abu Habiba, the client of al-Zubayr: I heard Hakim ibn Hizam say:

“I was born thirteen years before the Year of the Elephant, and I can remember when ʿAbd al-Muttalib intended to sacrifice his son ʿAbd Allah.”

Al-Waqidi related something similar and added: “That was five years before the birth of the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace).”

Hakim’s father was killed in the Fijar War, and Hakim took part in it.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar related that Hakim was born inside the Kaʿba. He said: He was one of the leading men of Quraysh and was a friend of the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) before the prophetic mission. He remained fond of him and loved him after the mission, but he delayed accepting Islam until he became Muslim in the Year of the Conquest.

It is established in the Sira and in the Sahih that he (may God bless him and grant him peace) said: “Whoever enters the house of Hakim ibn Hizam is safe.”

He was among those whose hearts were reconciled. He was present at Hunayn and was given one hundred camels from its spoils. His commitment to Islam then became excellent. He had been present at Badr with the unbelievers and escaped with those who escaped. Thus, whenever he wished to make a particularly solemn oath, he would say: “By Him who saved me on the day of Badr.” His kunya was Abu Khalid.

Al-Zubayr said: Islam came while the rifada—the office of provisioning the pilgrims—was in Hakim’s hands. He used to perform good deeds and maintain ties of kinship.

It is related in the Sahih that he asked the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace): “There are things I used to do during the Jahiliyya; will I receive a reward for them?” He replied: “You embraced Islam with the good you had previously done credited to you.” [1]

[1] Reported by Ahmad in al-Musnad, 3/402; al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra, 9/123 and 10/316; al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, 3/210, 213; Kanz al-ʿUmmal, hadith no. 1341; al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh al-Saghir, 70; and Muslim, 1/113–114, in the Book of Faith, chapter 55, “Clarification of the ruling concerning an unbeliever’s deeds,” hadith nos. 194 and 195.

Dar al-Nadwa was in his possession, and he later sold it to Muʿawiya for one hundred thousand dirhams. Ibn al-Zubayr reproached him, but he said to him: “My brother’s son, with it I have purchased a house in Paradise.” He then gave all the dirhams in charity. He was among those knowledgeable about the genealogies and historical reports of Quraysh.

He died in 50 AH; it is also said in 54 AH, in 58 AH, or in 60 AH. He was among those who lived for one hundred and twenty years, half of them in the Jahiliyya and [half] in Islam.

Al-Bukhari said in al-Tarikh: He died in the year 60 AH at the age of one hundred and twenty. Ibrahim ibn al-Mundhir said this. Al-Bukhari then transmitted, through ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUrwa, from ʿUrwa, who said: “He died ten years into the caliphate of Muʿawiya.”

entries.english_text:
2263—Khuzayma ibn Hakim al-Sulami «4»: al-Bahzi. He is also said to have been Ibn Thabit.

Ibn Shahin and others mentioned him, and Ibn Manda mentioned that he was related by marriage to Khadija, Mother of the Believers.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated in the Tafsir, by way of Abu Imran al-Jawni, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata, from Jabir, that Khuzayma ibn Thabit—not the Ansari—asked the Prophet ﷺ about “the secure city,” and he replied: “Mecca.”

Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat through this same chain in a very lengthy form. Its beginning states that he was in a caravan belonging to Khadija with the Prophet ﷺ, and he said to him: “O Muhammad, I see certain qualities in you, and I bear witness that you are the Prophet who will arise in Tihama. I have believed in you, and when I hear that you have come forth, I shall come to you.” He delayed coming to the Prophet ﷺ until the Day of the Conquest, when he came to him. Upon seeing him, he said: “Welcome to the first emigrant ...” The rest of the hadith follows.

He said: “No one narrated it from Ibn Jurayj except Abu Imran.”

Abu Musa said: “Abu Ma‘shar and Ubayd ibn Hakim narrated it from Ibn Jurayj, from al-Zuhri, as a mursal report; however, they called him Khuzayma ibn Hakim al-Sulami.”

Ibn Shahin likewise named him thus, through Yazid ibn Iyad, from al-Zuhri, who said: “Khuzayma ibn Hakam used to visit Khadija every year, and there was kinship between them. He came to her, and she sent him with the Prophet ﷺ ...” He related it at length, over two folios. It contains much that is unusual, and its isnad is extremely weak as well as interrupted.

We also transmitted it in Ibn Asakir’s Tarikh by way of Ubayd ibn Hakim, from Ibn Khurayj, in similarly lengthy form.

(1) Omitted from A.

(2) Asad al-Ghaba, entry (1451); al-Isti‘ab, entry (669).

(3) In A: “wa-laban Aba Umar.”

(4) Asad al-Ghaba, entry (1452).

It was also narrated from Mansur ibn al-Mu‘tamir, from Qabisa, from Khuzayma ibn Hakim.

uncertainties.issue: The punctuation leaves the exact syntactic relationship of al-Bahzi to the heading slightly unclear; it is most naturally an additional tribal nisba. “Ibn Thabit” is an explicitly reported variant identification.
uncertainties.best_rendering: al-Sulami: al-Bahzi. He is also said to have been Ibn Thabit.

uncertainties.issue: The Arabic sihr denotes a relation by marriage but, without further context, does not securely specify whether he was a son-in-law, brother-in-law, or another affine.
uncertainties.best_rendering: he was related by marriage to Khadija

uncertainties.issue: Gharib may describe unusual contents or hadith material transmitted through unfamiliar or isolated routes; the immediate wording does not determine a narrower technical sense.
uncertainties.best_rendering: It contains much that is unusual.

uncertainties.issue: The recorded reading is syntactically opaque and appears unrelated to the surrounding entry, likely because these apparatus notes overlap adjacent material. Translating it conjecturally would risk altering the witness evidence.
uncertainties.best_rendering: In A: “wa-laban Aba Umar.”

uncertainties.issue: The text reads Ibn Khurayj (خريج), whereas the earlier chains read Ibn Jurayj (جريج). This is probably a textual or typographical variant, but it has been preserved rather than silently normalized.
uncertainties.best_rendering: from Ibn Khurayj

uncertainties.location: Final sentence, “وروى عن منصور بن المعتمر”
uncertainties.issue: The subject of the active verb “narrated” is not explicit in the surviving wording. A passive English construction preserves the chain without supplying an uncertain narrator.
uncertainties.best_rendering: It was also narrated from Mansur ibn al-Mu‘tamir, from Qabisa, from Khuzayma ibn Hakim.

2847 Z—Zuhayr ibn Qunfudh al-Asadi:

Al-Fakihi mentioned him in Akhbar Makka, by way of Zakariyya, by way of Zakariyya ibn Qatan (2), from Safiyya bint Zuhayr ibn Qunfudh al-Asadiyya, from her father: the Prophet—may God bless him and grant him peace—would remain at Hira during the day, and when night came, he would descend from Hira. He would go to the mosque in the mountain pass, and Khadija would come to him from Mecca and meet him at the mosque in the mountain pass. Then, when dawn drew near, they would part.

(2) In A: Fatan.

uncertainties.best_rendering: the mosque in the mountain pass

entries.english_text:
2897—Zayd ibn Haritha (4): ibn Sharahil al-Ka‘bi.

His lineage has been given above in the entry on his son, Usama ibn Zayd. Ibn Sa‘d said: His mother was Su‘da bint Tha‘laba ibn Amir, of Banu Ma‘n of Tayy. [Ibn Umar said: We used to call Zayd ibn Haritha only Zayd ibn Muhammad, until the verse was revealed: “Call them by their fathers’ names” [al-Ahzab 33:5]—the hadith. Al-Bukhari transmitted it.] (5)

(1) Transmitted by al-Bukhari from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, 10/445 (6018), and Muslim 1/68 (75–47).

(2) Asad al-Ghaba, entry [1827]; al-Isti‘ab, entry [847].

(3) Al-Thiqat 3/141; Tajrid Asma al-Sahaba 1/197; al-Istibsar, 124; Tabaqat al-Huffaz, 93; Shadharat al-Dhahab 1/9; al-Tarikh al-Saghir 1/315; al-Wafi bi-l-Wafayat 15/25; Asad al-Ghaba, entry [1828].

(4) Asad al-Ghaba, entry [1829]; al-Isti‘ab [848]; Musnad Ahmad 4/161; Tabaqat Ibn Sa‘d 3/1/27; Tabaqat Khalifa, 6; Tarikh Khalifa, 86, 87; al-Tarikh al-Kabir 3/390; al-Tarikh al-Saghir 1/23; al-Jarh wa-l-Ta‘dil 3/559; Ibn Asakir 6/291, 1; Tahdhib al-Asma wa-l-Lughat 1/202, 203; Tahdhib al-Kamal, 453; al-‘Ibar 1/9; Majma‘ al-Zawa’id 9/274; al-‘Iqd al-Thamin 4/459, 473; Tahdhib al-Tahdhib 3/401; Khulasat Tadhhib al-Kamal, 127; Tahdhib Tarikh Ibn Asakir 5/454.

(5) This is not in A.

Hisham ibn Muhammad ibn al-Sa’ib al-Kalbi related to us, from his father and from Jamil ibn Marthad al-Ta’i and others, who said: Su‘da, the mother of Zayd ibn Haritha, visited her people with Zayd accompanying her. During the Jahiliyya, cavalry belonging to Banu al-Qayn ibn Jisr raided the dwellings of Banu Ma‘n. They carried off Zayd, who was then an adolescent boy, brought him to the market of Ukaz, and offered him for sale. Hakim ibn Hizam bought him for his paternal aunt Khadija for four hundred dirhams. When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, married her, she gave Zayd to him.

When his father, Haritha ibn Sharahil, lost him, he said:

I wept for Zayd, not knowing what befell him—
Is he alive, and thus still hoped for, or did death overtake him?

[al-Tawil meter]

Among verses in which he said:

I commend him to Amr and Qays, both of them,
And I commend him to Yazid, then after them to Jabal. (1) (2)

[al-Tawil meter]

By Amr and Qays he meant his own two brothers; by Yazid, Zayd’s maternal brother, namely Yazid ibn Ka‘b ibn Sharahil; and by Jabal, his eldest son.

He said: Some people from Kalb performed the pilgrimage. They saw Zayd, and he recognized them and they recognized him. He said, “Convey these verses to my family”:

I yearn for my people, though I am far away,
For I dwell beside the House, at the sacred ritual sites.

[al-Tawil meter]

This was among several verses.

They went and informed his father, describing Zayd’s location to him. Haritha and his brother Ka‘b set out with his ransom. They came to Mecca and asked about the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. They were told, “He is in the mosque.” They entered upon him and said, “O son of Abd al-Muttalib, O son of the master of his people! You are the people of Allah’s sanctuary: you release the captive and feed the prisoner. We have come to you concerning our son, who is your slave. Show us favor and deal generously concerning his ransom, for we shall offer you a generous payment.”

He asked, “Who is that?”

They replied, “Zayd ibn Haritha.”

He said, “Shall I offer you something other than that? Call him and give him the choice. If he chooses you, he is yours without ransom; but if he chooses me, then, by Allah, I am not one to accept a ransom for someone who has chosen me.”

They said, “You have treated us with more than justice.”

He summoned Zayd and asked, “Do you recognize these two?”

He answered, “Yes. This is my father, and this is my paternal uncle.”

He said, “You already know who I am, and you have seen my companionship with you. Choose me, or choose them.”

Zayd said, “I am not one who would choose anyone over you. To me, you hold the place of both father and paternal uncle.”

They said, “Woe to you, Zayd! Do you choose slavery over freedom, and over your father, your paternal uncle, and your household?”

He replied, “Yes. I have seen something from this man on account of which I would never choose anyone over him.”

When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, saw that, he took Zayd out to the Hijr and said, “Bear witness that Zayd is my son: he inherits from me, and I inherit from him.” When Zayd’s father and paternal uncle saw this, they were content, and they departed. He was thereafter called Zayd ibn Muhammad until Allah brought Islam.

Ibn Ishaq also related the story of Haritha, Zayd’s father, coming in search of him, in similar terms.

Ibn al-Kalbi said, from his father, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas: When the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, adopted Zayd, he married him to Zaynab bint Jahsh, the daughter of his paternal aunt Umayma bint Abd al-Muttalib. Before that, the Prophet had married him to his freedwoman Umm Ayman, who bore him Usama. Then, after he divorced Zaynab, the Prophet married him to Umm Kulthum bint Uqba. Her mother was Arwa bint Kurayz, whose mother was al-Bayda’ bint Abd al-Muttalib. Umm Kulthum bore him Zayd ibn Zayd and Ruqayya. He then divorced Umm Kulthum and married Durra bint Abi Lahab ibn Abd al-Muttalib. He divorced her and married Hind bint al-Awwam, the sister of al-Zubayr.

Ibn Umar said: We used to call Zayd ibn Haritha only Zayd ibn Muhammad, until the verse was revealed: “Call them by their fathers’ names” [al-Ahzab 33:5]—the hadith. Al-Bukhari transmitted it.

It is said that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, named him Zayd because Quraysh loved this name; it was the name of Qusayy. The account of his father’s coming to Mecca seeking his ransom has already been mentioned in his entry.

Abd al-Razzaq related from Ma‘mar, from al-Zuhri, who said: “We do not know of anyone who embraced Islam before Zayd ibn Haritha.” Abd al-Razzaq said: “No one other than al-Zuhri mentioned this.”

I say: Al-Waqidi mentioned it decisively through an isnad of his from Sulayman ibn Yasar. Za’ida also said it.

Zayd ibn Haritha witnessed Badr and the campaigns thereafter. He was killed in the expedition of Mu’ta while serving as commander. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, also left him in charge of Medina during some of his journeys.

It is related from al-Bara’ ibn Azib that Zayd ibn Haritha said, “O Messenger of Allah, you established a bond of brotherhood between me and Hamza.” Abu Ya‘la transmitted it.

It is related from Aisha: “The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, never sent Zayd ibn Haritha on an expedition without appointing him commander over its men. Had he survived, he would have appointed him his successor.” Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba transmitted it from her with a strong isnad.

Salama ibn al-Akwa‘ said: “I campaigned with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in seven campaigns, and with Zayd ibn Haritha in seven campaigns, on which the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed him commander over us.” Al-Bukhari transmitted it.

Al-Waqidi said: Zayd’s first expeditions were to al-Qarada (1), then to al-Jumum (2), then to al-‘Is (3), then to al-Taraf (4), then to Hisma, then to Umm Qirfa, followed by his appointment as commander of the expedition of Mu’ta. He was martyred there at the age of fifty-five. By agreement, no one is named by his personal name in the Quran except him—and then al-Sijill, if that is established.

It is related from Muhammad ibn Usama ibn Zayd, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said to Zayd ibn Haritha: “O Zayd, you are my mawla; you are of me and belong to me, and you are the person dearest to me.” Ibn Sa‘d transmitted it with a sound isnad. It is also found in Ahmad in a longer form.

Ibn Umar related that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “By Allah, he was indeed worthy of command”—meaning Zayd ibn Haritha—“and he was indeed among the people dearest to me.” Al-Bukhari transmitted it.

Al-Tirmidhi and others related from the hadith of Aisha, who said: “Zayd ibn Haritha arrived in Medina while the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was in my house. Zayd came to him and knocked at the door, whereupon he rose to meet him, embraced him, and kissed him.”

It is related from Ibn Umar: “Umar assigned Usama a larger stipend than he assigned me. I asked him about it, and he replied: ‘He was dearer to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, than you were, and his father was dearer to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, than your father was.’” Authentic.

(1) Al-Qarada: with all its consonants vowelled. It is a watering place below the waters of al-Thalabut in Najd, in al-Rumma, belonging to Banu Na‘ama. It is also said with fa, and has been mentioned previously. See Marasid al-Ittila‘ 3/1077.

(2) Al-Jumum: land belonging to Banu Sulaym. One of the Prophet’s expeditions took place there; he sent Zayd ibn Haritha against it as a raider. See Mu‘jam al-Buldan 2/190.

(3) Al-‘Is: with kasra; “one of what preceded it” [as the Arabic text reads]. It is a place in the lands of Banu Sulaym containing a watering place called Dhanaban al-‘Is, above al-Suraqiyya. Al-‘Is is also a fortress between Yanbu and al-Marwa. It is also said to be one of the districts of Medina on the seacoast. See Marasid al-Ittila‘ 2/975.

(4) Al-Taraf: with all its consonants vowelled, ending in fa. Al-Waqidi said: “Al-Taraf is a watering place near al-Marma, short of al-Nakhil, thirty-six miles from Medina.” Ibn Ishaq said: “Al-Taraf is in the direction of Iraq.” Taraf al-Qaddum—with the dal doubled and the qaf bearing damma—is a mountain pass in al-Sarat; it is properly pronounced without doubling, although hadith scholars double it. M 2/885.

Zayd ibn Haritha has a report in the Sahih, narrated by Anas from him, concerning the story of Zaynab bint Jahsh. Anas, al-Bara’ ibn Azib, Ibn Abbas, and his son Usama ibn Zayd narrated from him, while a group of the Successors transmitted reports from him without direct linkage.

(1) In T, the reading is “Bajal.”

(2) See the first and second verses in Asad al-Ghaba, entry no. 1829; the first and last of them in al-Isti‘ab, entry no. 848; and also Tabaqat 3/28 and Sirat Ibn Hisham 1/248.

entries.english_text:
4321 Z—al-Tahir:

Son of the lord of creation, Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim. His mother was Khadija bint Khuwaylid.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said, in the biography of Khadija in the Book of Genealogy: “My cousin Mus‘ab related to me, saying: Khadija bore the Prophet—may God bless him and grant him peace—al-Qasim and al-Tahir, who was also called al-Tayyib. Al-Tahir was born after the advent of prophethood and died young. His name was Abdullah [and he mentioned the four daughters].” (1)

Likewise, Yazid ibn Iyad, reporting from al-Zuhri, confined the sons to al-Qasim and Abdullah.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar transmitted it from Muhammad ibn Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Fulayh, from him. (2)

Al-Zubayr said: “Ibrahim ibn Hamza also related to me, saying: Khadija bore al-Qasim and al-Tahir—and, they say, Abdullah and al-Tayyib”; and he mentioned the daughters.

Through Ibn Lahi‘a, from Abu al-Aswad, the ward of Urwa, who said: “Khadija bore al-Qasim, al-Tayyib, al-Tahir, and Abdullah”; and he mentioned the daughters.

And through Abu Damra, from Abu Bakr ibn Uthman and others, that Khadija bore the four sons, whom they named, and the four daughters, whom they also named. He said: “As for the sons, they all died in Mecca. As for the daughters, they married and bore children.”

(1) Omitted in A.
(2) In A: “and he mentioned the four daughters.”

He said: “Muhammad ibn Fadala related to me, saying: Khadija bore him three sons: al-Qasim, al-Tahir, and Abdullah.” He said: “Ali ibn Salih related to me, from my grandfather Abdullah ibn Mus‘ab, that al-Zubayr’s mother Safiyya gave him the kunya Abu al-Tahir [after the name of] (1) her brother’s son, al-Tahir. After him, her brother [her son] (2) al-Zubayr bore that kunya. His son was one of the most elegant young men in Mecca, and after him the Messenger of God—may God bless him and grant him peace—named his own son.”

In al-Muwaffaqiyyat he related approximately the same from Muhammad ibn Fadala. It states that al-Tahir ibn al-Zubayr was born in al-Shi‘b, (3) and that the Prophet—may God bless him and grant him peace—named his son al-Tahir after him. [The remainder of his account will appear in the biography of Abdullah, God Most High willing.] (4)

The letter ta, followed by fa and lam.

(1) Omitted in A.
(2) Omitted in A.
(3) In A: “died.”
(4) Omitted in T.

uncertainties.issue: The pronoun “him” is not explicit in the Arabic chain; al-Zuhri is the most likely antecedent.
uncertainties.best_rendering: from Muhammad ibn Hasan, from Muhammad ibn Fulayh, from him

uncertainties.location: Report from Ali ibn Salih: “her brother [her son] al-Zubayr”
uncertainties.issue: The transmitted wording is grammatically and genealogically difficult. The bracketed “her son” is absent from manuscript A and stands beside “her brother,” leaving the intended kinship designation uncertain.
uncertainties.best_rendering: her brother [her son] al-Zubayr

uncertainties.location: Report from Ali ibn Salih: “His son was … and after him …”
uncertainties.issue: The antecedents of the masculine pronouns are not fully explicit. The parallel report in al-Muwaffaqiyyat supports understanding the referent as al-Tahir ibn al-Zubayr.
uncertainties.best_rendering: His son was one of the most elegant young men in Mecca, and after him the Messenger of God named his own son.

uncertainties.location: al-Muwaffaqiyyat report concerning al-Tahir ibn al-Zubayr
uncertainties.issue: The main text reads “was born in al-Shi‘b,” while manuscript A reads “died.” Al-Shi‘b may designate a specific Meccan quarter or mountain pass, but the text does not identify it more precisely.
uncertainties.best_rendering: was born in al-Shi‘b; variant in A: “died”

entries.english_text:
5602—Afif al-Kindi [4]

A paternal cousin of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays. It is also said that he was his paternal uncle; al-Tabari stated this categorically.

It is also said that he was his brother. The majority hold that he was his paternal cousin and his maternal brother, and Abu Nu'aym stated this categorically.

Ibn Hibban said, “He had Companionship.” Al-Tabari said, “His name was Shurahbil, and Afif was a sobriquet.” Al-Jahiz said, “His name was Sharahil, and he was surnamed Afif because of his words in some verses:

She said to me, ‘Come, then, to youthful dalliance!’
But I said, ‘I have abstained from that which you know.’

[al-Wafir meter]

Al-Baghawi, Abu Ya'la, al-Nasa'i in al-Khasa'is, and al-Uqayli in al-Du'afa' transmitted, by way of Asad ibn Wada'a, from Ibn Yahya ibn Afif, from his father, from his grandfather, who said:

“I came to Mecca during the Age of Ignorance, intending to make purchases for my family. I went to al-Abbas, and while I was sitting with him, looking at the Ka'ba, when the sun had risen high in the sky, a young man came and faced the Ka'ba. Before long, a boy came and stood on his right, and then a woman came and stood behind them. The young man bowed, and the boy and the woman bowed; then they rose, and then they prostrated. I said, ‘O Abbas, this is a momentous affair!’ He said, ‘Indeed.’ I said, ‘Who is this?’ He said, ‘This is Muhammad ibn Abd Allah, my brother’s son; this boy is Ali, my brother’s son; and this woman is Khadija. He has informed me that the Lord of the heavens and the earth has commanded him to follow this religion. By God, there is no one on the entire earth following this religion other than these three.’”

Afif said, “I wished that I could have been their fourth.” Ibn Abd al-Barr said, “This is a very fine hadith.”

I say: It has another route, transmitted by al-Bukhari in his al-Tarikh, al-Baghawi, Ibn Abi Khaythama, Ibn Manda, and the author of al-Ghaylaniyyat, all by way of Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim ibn Sa'd, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: Yahya ibn Abi al-Ash'ath related to me, from Isma'il ibn Iyas ibn Afif, from his father, from his grandfather. He then related something similar and said at its conclusion: “No one followed him in his affair except his wife and his paternal cousin, while he claims that the treasures of Chosroes and Caesar will be opened to him.” After Afif had embraced Islam, he used to say, “Had God granted me Islam that day, I would have been the second alongside Ali.”

Al-Bukhari said, “He is not corroborated in this.” Al-Hakim transmitted it in al-Mustadrak through this same route, except that his version has “from Isma'il ibn Amr ibn Afif,” substituting Amr for Iyas.

Ibn Fathun said concerning this Afif, “Al-Bawardi vocalized his name in the diminutive, while the form most commonly spoken has an a-vowel.”

I say: Its reading in sound manuscripts of Mu'jam al-Baghawi is as al-Bawardi vocalized it.

Editorial notes printed with the entry:

(1) In A: “Afif ibn Nubayh.”

(2) In A: “The son of al-Hajjaj, Abu Amir …”

(3) “It is said, and Ibrahim was …”; in A: “al-Amir, the son of Abu Salama ibn Abd Allah ibn Afif ibn Nubayh ibn al-Hajjaj.”

(4) Usd al-Ghaba, entry 3702; al-Isti'ab, entry 2059; al-Thiqat, 3/311; al-Istibsar, 351; al-Jarh wa-l-Ta'dil, 7/29; Tajrid Asma' al-Sahaba, 1/383; al-Ikmal, 6/226; al-Tarikh al-Kabir, 7/75; Khulasat Tadhhib, 2/235; Taqrib al-Tahdhib, 2/25; Tahdhib al-Tahdhib, 7/236; Tahdhib al-Kamal, 2/943; Tabsir al-Muntabih, 3/957.

(5) In J: “Afif lima.”

(1, following-page note) In A: “Anis.”

names.arabic: أبو سلمة بن عبد اللَّه بن عفيف بن نبيه بن الحجاج
names.english: Abu Salama ibn Abd Allah ibn Afif ibn Nubayh ibn al-Hajjaj

uncertainties.best_rendering: But I said, “I have abstained from that which you know.”

uncertainties.issue: These notes appear to belong to text on the preceding page or entry, and notes (2)–(3) are syntactically fragmentary without that lost context.
uncertainties.best_rendering: They are translated literally as detached editorial fragments and are not integrated into entry 5602’s narrative.

uncertainties.best_rendering: In J: “Afif lima.”

uncertainties.issue: The grammatical subject is unstated; it may refer to the immediate transmitter or more generally to the report’s lack of corroboration.
uncertainties.best_rendering: He is not corroborated in this.

uncertainties.best_rendering: Afif in the heading and narrative; al-Bawardi’s alternative is described as the diminutive Ufayf.

entries.english_text:
7284 — al-Qasim, son of our master, the Messenger of God—may God bless him and grant him peace—(1):

[He was] his firstborn, the first child born to him, and it was after him that he took his kunya.

He was born before the prophetic mission and died young. It is also said that he died after reaching the age of discernment. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said: Muhammad ibn Nadla (2) related to me, from one of the shaykhs, who said: Khadija gave birth to al-Qasim, and he lived until he could walk.

Ibn Sa'd transmitted, by way of Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im: Al-Qasim died when he was two years old.

He also related something similar from Qatada, while Mujahid said that he lived for seven days. Al-Fadl al-Ala'i said: He lived for seventeen months after the prophetic mission.

Yunus ibn Bukayr transmitted in the Additions to al-Maghazi, from Abu Abd Allah al-Ju'fi—he is Jabir—from Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn: Al-Qasim had reached the age at which he could mount a riding animal and travel upon a select she-camel. When he died, al-As ibn Wa'il said, “Muhammad has now become cut off.” Then there was revealed: “Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar—as compensation for your affliction through al-Qasim, O Muhammad.” This indicates that al-Qasim died after the prophetic mission.

Likewise, Ibn Majah, al-Tayalisi, and al-Harbi transmitted, by way of Fatima bint al-Husayn, from her father, who said: When al-Qasim died, Khadija said, “O Messenger of God, al-Qasim's little portion of milk has come in. If only God had kept him alive until he completed his suckling.” He said, “The completion of his suckling is in Paradise.”

Al-Harbi said: She meant that she grieved for him until her milk flowed for him.

In Sunan Ibn Majah, after the words, “He did not complete his suckling,” it reads: She said, “If I knew that, O Messenger of God, what happened to him would be easier for me.” He replied, “If you wish, I shall pray to God and let you hear his voice.” She said, “Rather, God and His Messenger have spoken the truth.”

This is very clear in indicating that he died during Islam, but there is weakness in the chain of transmission. As for Abu Nu'aym's statement, “I do not know of anyone among our early authorities who mentioned him among the Companions,” al-Bukhari did mention in al-Tarikh al-Awsat, by way of Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Hisham ibn Urwa, that al-Qasim died before Islam. However, there will come, in the entry on Fatima bint Asad, the hadith: “No one was spared the compression of the grave except Fatima bint Asad.” It was asked, “Not even al-Qasim?” He replied, “Not al-Qasim, nor Ibrahim.” Ibrahim was the younger of the two. This, together with the report of Fatima bint al-Husayn, indicates the contrary of Hisham ibn Urwa's narration.

(1) Usd al-Ghaba, t. (4252).

(2) In A: Fadala.

(3) Al-labna is a small portion of milk, and al-labna [presumably al-lubayna] is its diminutive. Al-Nihaya, 4/228.

names.english: our master, the Messenger of God (Muhammad)

uncertainties.issue: The reading «وبكرة» is grammatically anomalous in context and is likely a corruption or typographical rendering of «وبكره» (“his firstborn”), which is then restated by «وأول مولود له».
uncertainties.best_rendering: [He was] his firstborn, the first child born to him.

uncertainties.issue: Witness A reads «فضالة» in place of «نضلة».
uncertainties.best_rendering: Muhammad ibn Nadla; A reads Fadala.

uncertainties.issue: The transmitted wording repeats «اللبنة», although the intended diminutive, matching the entry's «لبينة», is apparently «اللبينة».
uncertainties.best_rendering: Al-labna is a small portion of milk, and al-lubayna is its diminutive.

entries.english_text:
8302—Maysara:

Khadija’s servant.

He is mentioned in the Sira. He accompanied the Prophet ﷺ on Khadija’s trading expedition before the Prophet married her. He related some of the proofs of the Prophet’s prophethood. Ibn Asakir included a biographical notice for him. I have not found an explicit report stating that he remained alive until the beginning of the prophetic mission, so I have included him on that possibility.

uncertainties.issue: The word غلام can mean a boy, young man, servant, or enslaved male; the precise legal status is not explicit here.
uncertainties.best_rendering: Khadija’s servant.

uncertainties.issue: Literally, “remained until the mission”; in context this most likely means that he remained alive until the beginning of Muhammad’s prophetic mission.
uncertainties.best_rendering: remained alive until the beginning of the prophetic mission

entries.english_text:
8695—Nabbash ibn Zarara (1)

Ibn Manda said: “He is mentioned in the accounts of the military campaigns. He accompanied the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him).” This is how he mentioned him, briefly.

Abu Musa said: “Nabbash ibn Zarara al-Tamimi, Abu Hala: al-Mustaghfiri included him among the Companions in the chapter on the letter nun.” Ibn al-Athir took him to task over this and set forth his genealogy, saying: “Ibn Zarara ibn Waqdan ibn Habib ibn Salama ibn Adi ibn Jurwa ibn Usayyid ibn Amr ibn Tamim, Abu Hala al-Tamimi.” He then said: “Musab al-Zubayri said: ‘He was a confederate of Banu Abd al-Dar.’” Ibn al-Athir said: “Abu Musa added him as a supplement to Ibn Manda, although Ibn Manda had already mentioned him; thus there was no reason to add him. Moreover, he did not have the status of a Companion, for he lived before the Prophethood: he was Khadija’s husband before the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and she bore Abu Hala to him. Neither Zarara nor his son had the status of a Companion.” End quote.

As for his criticism of Abu Musa, it is well directed, because Abu Musa gave Nabbash the kunya Abu Hala and said that he was a Tamimi. His criticism of Ibn Manda, however, is open to question, because Ibn Manda did not set forth the man’s genealogy; it was therefore possible that he was another person. For this reason Abu Musa added him, attributing the notice to al-Mustaghfiri. Al-Mustaghfiri’s basis for mentioning him was what he related through Musab al-Zubayri, who said: “Nabbash ibn Zarara al-Tamimi, Abu Hala, a confederate of Banu Abd al-Dar, was the father of Hind, Khadija’s son.” End quote, abridged.

Nothing in this indicates that he had the status of a Companion, because Musab was discussing genealogies simply as genealogies, not specifically from the standpoint of identifying the Companions.

(1) Asad al-Ghaba, entry no. 5195.

names.arabic: زرارة بن وقدان بن حبيب بن سلامة بن عدي بن جروة بن أسيّد بن عمرو بن تميم
names.english: Zarara ibn Waqdan ibn Habib ibn Salama ibn Adi ibn Jurwa ibn Usayyid ibn Amr ibn Tamim

uncertainties.best_rendering: she bore Abu Hala to him

uncertainties.location: “Neither Zarara nor his son had the status of a Companion”
uncertainties.issue: The wording explicitly names Zarara and his son, although the surrounding discussion concerns Nabbash ibn Zarara and may create uncertainty about the intended referents.
uncertainties.best_rendering: Neither Zarara nor his son had the status of a Companion

uncertainties.issue: The construction literally identifies Hind as Khadija’s son. It may be understood genealogically as Hind ibn Abi Hala, who was Khadija’s son, but the supplied Arabic does not state ibn Abi Hala here.
uncertainties.best_rendering: Hind, Khadija’s son

uncertainties.issue: The unvocalized genealogical name may admit variant vocalization; “Usayyid” is the strongest conventional rendering.
uncertainties.best_rendering: Usayyid

entries.english_text:
8907—Nabbash ibn Zurara al-Tamimi¹

Abu Hala, Khadija’s husband before the Prophet—may God bless him and grant him peace—the father of Hind, and the maternal uncle of al-Hasan ibn Ali.

Al-Mustaghfiri mentioned him, and Abu Musa followed him in the Supplement. This is an error.

¹ Usd al-Ghaba, t (5195).

uncertainties.issue: The siglum ت most likely abbreviates tarjama, indicating an entry or biographical notice number, but its expansion is not explicit in the supplied Arabic.
uncertainties.best_rendering: Usd al-Ghaba, t (5195).

entries.english_text:
8912 — Nastur the Monk

Ibn Sa‘d related from al-Waqidi that, when Khadija entered into an agreement with the Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—before the mission, and before he married her, concerning a trading journey to al-Sham, she sent her servant Maysara with him. Maysara related that the two of them arrived at Busra and stopped beneath the shade of a tree. Nastur the monk said to him, “No one has ever stopped beneath this tree except a prophet.” Then an altercation occurred between the Prophet—peace and blessings be upon him—and another man. The man said to him, “Swear by al-Lat and al-‘Uzza.” He replied, “I have never sworn by them; indeed, whenever I pass by them, I turn away from them.” The man then said to Maysara, “This is the prophet of this community.”

(1) Usd al-Ghaba, t. (5195).
(2) Usd al-Ghaba, t. (5198); al-Isti‘ab, t. (2688).
(3) Usd al-Ghaba, t. (5207); al-Isti‘ab, t. (2689).

I say: The story of Buhayra has already appeared under the single-dotted letter ba, in approximately the same form as the story of Nastur. It is better known as the story of Buhayra. On that account, Ibn Manda included Buhayra among the Companions; thus, this one meets his criterion.

uncertainties.location: First paragraph: «لما فاوضت النبي ... في تجارة إلى الشام»
uncertainties.issue: The verb «فاوضت» can mean that Khadija negotiated or conferred with the Prophet; in context it appears to denote reaching a commercial arrangement with him for the journey.
uncertainties.best_rendering: when Khadija entered into an agreement with the Prophet ... concerning a trading journey to al-Sham

uncertainties.issue: The editorial siglum «ت» most likely abbreviates «ترجمة» and designates a numbered biographical entry, but its exact expansion depends on the cited edition.
uncertainties.best_rendering: t. (5195), etc., preserving the editorial siglum

entries.english_text:
8935 — Hala ibn Abi Hala al-Tamimi (1)

Abu Umar said: He had Companionship. Ibn Hibban said: Hala, son of Khadija, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, had Companionship. The name of Abu Hala was Hind ibn al-Nabbash ibn Zurara ibn Waqdan ibn Habib ibn Salama ibn Ghudayy ibn Jarda ibn Usayyid—the last name being in the diminutive form and pronounced with gemination—ibn Amr ibn Tamim.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said: The name of Abu Hala was Malik ibn al-Nabbash; the remainder of the genealogy is the same. It is also said that his name was Zurara.

In this genealogy, Ibn Makula vocalized Ghudayy in the diminutive form, and he related that al-Zubayr gave it according to the ordinary form. The correct form is the diminutive.

Al-Tabarani transmitted from Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Tamim, from Zayd ibn Hala ibn Abi Hala al-Tamimi in Egypt: “My father related to me, from his father Tamim, from his father Zayd ibn Hala, from his father Hala ibn Abi Hala, that he came in to see the Prophet ﷺ while he was asleep. He awoke, drew Hala to his breast, and said, ‘Hala! Hala! Hala!’”

Jafar al-Mustaghfiri transmitted, by way of Mu’ammal ibn Ismail, from Hammad ibn Salama, from Hisham, from his father, from Aisha, who said: “A son of Khadija called Hala arrived while the Prophet ﷺ was taking his midday rest. During his rest he heard ‘Hala,’ so he awoke and said, ‘Hala! Hala!’”

Jafar said: Musa ibn Ismail differed from him, relating from Hammad with this isnad: “Hala was Khadija’s sister.” Jafar said: “This is the correct version.” End quote.

Hala, Khadija’s sister, has indeed been mentioned by way of Ali ibn Mushir, from Hisham, from his father, from Aisha, in the Sahih.

(1) al-Thiqat 3/437; Tajrid Asma al-Sahaba 2/116; Usd al-Ghaba, t. (5329); al-Tabaqat al-Kubra 8/19; al-Iqd al-Thamin 7/362; al-Isti‘ab, t. (2739).

names.arabic: علي بن محمد بن عمرو بن تميم
names.english: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Tamim

names.arabic: زيد بن هالة بن أبي هالة التميمي
names.english: Zayd ibn Hala ibn Abi Hala al-Tamimi

uncertainties.location: The statement concerning Ibn Makula’s vocalization of غذيّ
uncertainties.issue: The expression كالجادة literally indicates the ordinary or standard form, but the unvocalized text does not make the precise contrasting pronunciation explicit.
uncertainties.best_rendering: al-Zubayr gave it according to the ordinary form

uncertainties.location: The isnad beginning with Zayd ibn Hala ibn Abi Hala al-Tamimi in Egypt
uncertainties.issue: As transmitted, the chain repeats the names Zayd and Hala across generations and includes “from his father Tamim.” The genealogy may appear irregular, but it has been preserved exactly rather than harmonized.
uncertainties.best_rendering: from Zayd ibn Hala ibn Abi Hala al-Tamimi in Egypt: “My father related to me, from his father Tamim, from his father Zayd ibn Hala, from his father Hala ibn Abi Hala”

uncertainties.issue: قال هالة أخت خديجة can be punctuated either as the report’s wording, “Hala was Khadija’s sister,” or as “he said: Hala, Khadija’s sister.” The following judgment and reference to the Sahih support the former.
uncertainties.best_rendering: Hala was Khadija’s sister

entries.english_text:
9027—Hind ibn Abi Hala al-Tamimi[1]

The stepson of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him); his mother was Khadija, the wife of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him).

He transmitted from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). Al-Hasan ibn Ali transmitted from him the description of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him). Al-Tirmidhi, al-Baghawi, al-Tabarani, and others transmitted it through several routes from al-Hasan ibn Ali. It also reached us with an elevated—that is, short—chain in the Mashyakha of Abu Ali ibn Shadhan, through the route of the Ahl al-Bayt.

Al-Baghawi also transmitted it, and Ibn Manda transmitted it by way of Yaqub al-Taymi, from Ibn Abbas, who said to Hind ibn Abi Hala, “Describe the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) to me.” Al-Baghawi related from his uncle, from Abu Ubayd: The name of Abu Hala, Khadija’s husband before the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), was al-Nabbash ibn Zarara, and his son was Hind ibn al-Nabbash ibn Zarara ibn Waqdan ibn Habib ibn Salama ibn Ghadi ibn Jarda ibn Usayyid ibn Amr ibn Tamim, a confederate of the Banu Abd al-Dar. It is also said that he was Zarara ibn al-Nabbash.

Al-Zubayr said: His name was Malik ibn al-Nabbash ibn Zarara. Abu Muhammad ibn Hazm said: Abu Hala’s name was Hind ibn Zarara ibn al-Nabbash. I found an earlier authority who held the same view: Ibn Abi Khaythama said, “Ahmad ibn al-Miqdam narrated to us; Zuhayr ibn al-Ala narrated to us; Said narrated to us; Qatada said: Abu Hala was Hind ibn Zarara ibn al-Nabbash.” I saw in al-Marzubani’s Mu'jam al-Shu'ara that Zarara ibn al-Nabbash composed an elegy for the unbelievers of Badr, but al-Marzubani did not mention that he embraced Islam.

Ibn al-Sakan and Ibn Qani transmitted, by way of Sayf ibn Umar, from Abd Allah ibn Muhammad, from Hind ibn Hind ibn Abi Hala, from his father, who said: “I asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, what caused you to take your daughter away from Utayba’—meaning Ibn Abi Lahab—‘thereby provoking him against you?’ He replied, ‘Allah would not allow me to marry, or to give anyone in marriage, except to the people of Paradise.’”

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said: Hind was killed alongside Ali on the Day of the Camel. Al-Daraqutni said the same in Kitab al-Ikhwa. Abu Umar said: He was eloquent and articulate; he described the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), and did so excellently and precisely.

[1] Usd al-Ghaba, t. 5411; al-Isti'ab, t. 2737.

names.english: the Prophet Muhammad / the Messenger of Allah

names.arabic: هند بن النباش بن زرارة بن وقدان بن حبيب بن سلامة بن غدي بن جردة بن أسيد بن عمرو بن تميم

names.arabic: هند بن هند بن أبي هالة
names.english: Hind ibn Hind ibn Abi Hala
Mashyakhah of Abu Ali ibn Shadhan

uncertainties.issue: The pronoun may refer specifically to Ibn Hazm or more generally to the preceding identification of Abu Hala; the expression means that Ibn Hajar found an earlier precedent or authority for that view.
uncertainties.best_rendering: I found an earlier authority who held the same view.

uncertainties.issue: The unvocalized names غدي and جردة admit more than one Latin vocalization; the Arabic wording is clear, but the precise conventional spelling requires external prosopographical evidence.
uncertainties.best_rendering: Ghadi ibn Jarda

uncertainties.issue: The clause can mean that the Prophet’s action provoked Utayba against him or set Utayba upon him; the causal nuance is clear, but the exact idiomatic force is slightly uncertain.
uncertainties.best_rendering: thereby provoking him against you

entries.english_text:
9151—Waraqa ibn Nawfal ibn Asad⁴

Ibn Abd al-Uzza ibn Qusayy, al-Qurashi al-Asadi, the paternal cousin of Khadija, the wife of the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace).

Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Qani, Ibn al-Sakan, and others included him among the Companions. All of them transmitted, through Rawh ibn Musafir—one of the weak transmitters—from al-Amash, from Abd Allah ibn Abd Allah, from:

(1) Usd al-Ghaba, entry 5462.

(2) Usd al-Ghaba, entry 5460.

(3) Usd al-Ghaba, entry 5464.

(4) Usd al-Ghaba, entry 5465.

Said ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, from Waraqa ibn Nawfal, who said: I said, “O Muhammad, what is the one who comes to you like when he comes to you?” He replied: “He comes to me from heaven. His two wings are of pearl, and the soles of his feet are green.”¹

Ibn Asakir said: “Ibn Abbas did not hear from Waraqa, and I know of no one who said that he embraced Islam.”

Al-Tabari distinguished the subject of this hadith from Waraqa ibn Nawfal al-Asadi. The story, however, differs from the story of Waraqa found in the two Sahihs, through al-Zuhri, from Urwa, from Aisha: “The first thing with which the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) was begun…”—the hadith concerning Gabriel’s coming at Hira. It contains:

“Khadija then took him to Waraqa ibn Nawfal ibn Asad ibn Abd al-Uzza, Khadija’s paternal cousin. He had adopted Christianity during the pre-Islamic period…”—the hadith.

It also contains: “Waraqa said, ‘This is the Namus² who was sent down to Moses. Would that I were a strong young man then! Would that I might be alive when your people drive you out.’” At its end it says: “It was not long before Waraqa died.” The apparent meaning is that he affirmed his prophethood, but he died before—“Bahira” appears here in the text—the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) called the people to Islam; his case would therefore be like that of Bahira.

There is some question about establishing Companion status for him. Nevertheless, in the additions to al-Maghazi, in the recension of Yunus ibn Bukayr, from Ibn Ishaq, Yunus ibn Bukayr said, from Yunus ibn Amr—namely Ibn Abi Ishaq al-Sabii—from his father, from his grandfather, from Abu Maysara, whose name was Amr ibn Sharahbil and who was one of the senior Successors: The Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) said to Khadija, “When I withdraw by myself, I hear a call, and, by God, I have become afraid for myself.” She replied, “God forbid! God would never do that to you. By God, you faithfully discharge trusts…”—the hadith.

Waraqa said to him: “Receive glad tidings, and again receive glad tidings! I testify that you are the one whose coming the Son of Mary announced; that you follow a Namus like the Namus of Moses; that you are a messenger-prophet; and that, after this day of yours, you will assuredly be commanded to wage jihad. If I live to see that, I shall certainly fight alongside you.” When Waraqa died, the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) said: “I saw the priest in Paradise, wearing garments of silk, because he believed in me and affirmed my truthfulness.”³

(1) Abu Nuaym, Dalaʾil al-Nubuwwa, 1/72, and Tarikh Isfahan, 1/262.

(2) The Namus is the keeper of the king’s secret: specifically, the intimate confidant whom he acquaints with secrets that he conceals from others. It is also said that the Namus is the keeper of the secret of goodness. He meant Gabriel (peace be upon him), because God Most High singled him out for revelation and knowledge of the unseen, of which He informs no one else. Al-Nihaya, 5/119.

(3) Al-Bayhaqi transmitted it in Dalaʾil al-Nubuwwa, 2/158, from Abu Maysara Amr ibn Sharahbil…—the hadith. Al-Bayhaqi said: “This report has a break in its chain. If it is reliably preserved, it may be a report about its revelation after ‘Recite in the name of your Lord’ and ‘O you who are cloaked’ had been revealed to him. God knows best.” This is al-Bayhaqi’s wording. The report is mursal, contains something unusual, and implies that al-Fatiha was the first thing revealed.

Al-Bayhaqi transmitted it in al-Dalaʾil through this route and said: “This report has a break in its chain.”

I say: It is supported by what al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar transmitted: Uthman related to us, from al-Dahhak ibn Uthman, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Zinad, from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, who said: Bilal belonged to a slave woman of Banu Jumah. They used to torture him on the sun-scorched ground of Mecca, pressing his back against the burning ground so that he would associate partners with God, but he would say, “One, One!” Waraqa would pass him while he was in that condition and say, “One, One, O Bilal! By God, if you kill him, I shall surely make him a hanan.”¹

This is a good mursal report indicating that Waraqa remained alive until the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) called people to Islam and Bilal embraced Islam. This can be reconciled with Aisha’s hadith by understanding the statement “It was not long before Waraqa died” to mean that he died before Islam became widely known and before the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) was commanded to wage jihad.

What Muhammad ibn Aidh transmitted in al-Maghazi, however, presents a difficulty for that interpretation. Through Uthman ibn Ata al-Khurasani, from his father, from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, in the account of the beginning of revelation—which includes the story of Khadija and Waraqa in approximately the form of Aisha’s hadith—it says at the end: “If it is indeed he, and he then proclaims his call while I am alive, I shall assuredly give God a fine demonstration of myself in obedience to His Messenger and in supporting him well.” Waraqa died adhering to Christianity—so he said—but Uthman is weak.

Al-Zubayr said: Waraqa had come to detest the worship of idols, sought the true religion throughout the lands, and read the scriptures. Khadija used to ask him about the Prophet’s affair, and he would tell her: “I can only regard him as the prophet of this community whose coming Moses and Jesus announced.”

In Ibn Ishaq’s al-Maghazi al-Kabir—and al-Hakim cited it through Ibn Ishaq’s route—he said: Abd al-Malik ibn Abd Allah ibn Abi Sufyan ibn al-Ala ibn Haritha al-Thaqafi, who had been his shepherd, related to me, saying: Waraqa ibn Nawfal said, concerning what Khadija had told him about the affair of the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace):

O men! The vicissitudes of time and destiny!

[al-Basit meter]—the verses, among which are:

This Khadija comes to me that I may inform her,
Yet we possess no report of the hidden unseen.

That Ahmad will come to him, and Gabriel will tell him:
“You have been sent to humankind.”

I said: Perhaps the God in whom you place your hope will fulfill it for him;
So hope for good and wait.

[al-Basit meter]

(1) Hanan means mercy and compassion; hanan also means provision and blessing. He meant: “I shall make his grave a place of hanan,” that is, a place where God’s mercy may be expected, and I shall touch it seeking blessing, just as people touch the graves of the righteous from former communities who were killed in God’s path. That would rebound upon you as disgrace and a source of public reproach. Waraqa followed the religion of Jesus (peace be upon him) and died shortly before the Prophet’s mission, for he said to the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace): “If I live to see your day, I shall certainly support you with mighty support.” There is, however, a problem with this, since Bilal was not tortured until after he embraced Islam. Al-Nihaya, 1/452.

Ibn Adi transmitted in al-Kamil, through Ismail ibn Mujalid, from his father, from al-Shabi, from Jabir, from the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace): “I saw Waraqa in the midst of Paradise, wearing fine silk.”

Ibn Adi said: “Ismail alone transmitted it from his father.”

I say: Ibn al-Sakan transmitted it through Yahya ibn Said al-Umawi, from Mujalid, but his wording is: “I saw Waraqa beside one of the rivers of Paradise, because he used to say, ‘My religion is Zayd’s religion, and my God is Zayd’s God.’”

Muhammad ibn Abi Shayba transmitted it through this route in his Tarikh. Al-Bazzar transmitted, through Abu Muawiya, from Hisham ibn Urwa, from his father, from Aisha, who said: “The Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) forbade reviling Waraqa.”

It also appears in Yunus ibn Bukayr’s additions to al-Maghazi. He transmitted it from Hisham ibn Urwa, from his father, who said: A brother of Waraqa exchanged insults with a man. The man then turned upon Waraqa and reviled him. This reached the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace), and he said: “Do you not know that I saw for Waraqa a garden—or two gardens?” He therefore forbade reviling him.

Al-Bazzar also transmitted it through Abu Usama, from Hisham, as a mursal report.

Ahmad transmitted, through Ibn Lahiʿa, from Abu al-Aswad, from Urwa, from Aisha, that Khadija asked the Prophet (may God bless him and grant him peace) about Waraqa ibn Nawfal. He replied: “I saw him, and I saw that he was wearing white garments. I reckon that, had he been one of the inhabitants of the Fire, he would not have been wearing white garments.”

uncertainties.issue: The canonical text reads «مات قبل أن يدعو بحيرا رسول الله الناس إلى الإسلام». The occurrence of «بحيرا» before «رسول الله» is syntactically disruptive and is probably an intrusive or corrupt reading; the sense evidently requires “before the Messenger of God called people to Islam,” followed by the comparison with Bahira.
uncertainties.best_rendering: “but he died before—‘Bahira’ appears here in the text—the Messenger of God called the people to Islam; his case would therefore be like that of Bahira.”

uncertainties.issue: The noun «حنانا» has several possible senses. The accompanying footnote interprets it as making Bilal’s grave a locus of mercy or blessing, rather than merely showing him compassion.
uncertainties.best_rendering: “I shall surely make him a hanan,” retaining the Arabic term and translating the supplied explanation in full.

entries.english_text:
10182—Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi

Ibn Abd al-Uzza (1) ibn Abd Shams ibn Abd Manaf al-Abshami. His mother was Hala bint Khuwaylid, and he was nicknamed Jarw al-Batha (“the Whelp of al-Batha”).

(1) Durr al-Sahaba, 782; al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, 2/18, 8/30.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said: He was called al-Amin. There was disagreement concerning his name. It was said to be Laqit—this was stated by Musab al-Zubayri, Amr ibn Ali al-Fallas, al-Alai, al-Hakim Abu Ahmad, and others, and al-Baladhuri considered it the preferable view. It was also said to be al-Zubayr; al-Zubayr related this from Uthman ibn al-Dahhak. It was said to be Hushaym, as related by Ibn Abd al-Barr. It was also said to be Mihsham—with the first letter bearing kasra, the second quiescent, and the dotted shin bearing fatha; and it was said to be Muhashshim—with the first letter bearing damma, the second fatha, and the doubled shin kasra—as related by al-Zubayr and al-Baghawi.

Ibn Manda related—and Abu Nuaym followed him—that it was said that his name was Yasir, but I think this is a corruption of Yasim.

Before the prophetic mission, according to what al-Zubayr related from his uncle Musab—and as some learned people asserted—he was bound in brotherhood with the Messenger of God ﷺ and frequently visited him in his home. The Messenger married him to his daughter Zaynab, the eldest of his daughters, who was the daughter of Abu al-As’s maternal aunt Khadija. It nevertheless happened that he did not accept Islam until after the Hijra.

Ibn Ishaq said: He was one of the men of Mecca renowned for wealth, trustworthiness, and commerce.

Al-Hakim Abu Ahmad transmitted with a sound chain from al-Shabi, who said: Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ, was married to Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi. She emigrated while Abu al-As remained upon his religion. It happened that he set out for Syria on a trading journey. When he was near Medina, some Muslims wanted to go out against him, seize what he had, and kill him. News of this reached Zaynab, and she said, “O Messenger of God, are not the Muslims’ compact and covenant one?”

He said, “Yes.” She said, “Then bear witness that I have granted protection to Abu al-As.” When the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ saw this, they went out to him unarmed and without weapons. They said to him, “O Abu al-As, you are a man of high standing among Quraysh, and you are the cousin and son-in-law of the Messenger of God ﷺ. Would you accept Islam and thereby acquire as booty the property of the people of Mecca that is with you?” He said, “Evil indeed is what you have instructed me to do: to renounce my religion through an act of treachery.” He continued until he reached Mecca and delivered to every person entitled to something his due. [The narrator] said: Then he said, saying, “O people of Mecca, have I discharged my obligation?” They said, “By God, yes.” He then said, “I bear witness that there is no deity but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.” He then came to Medina as an emigrant, and the Messenger of God ﷺ restored his wife to him under the original marriage contract.

Notwithstanding the soundness of its chain as far as al-Shabi, this is a mursal report, and it is anomalous, being contradicted by a report more firmly established than it. In Ibn Ishaq’s al-Maghazi, there is: Yahya ibn Abbad ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr related to me, from his father, from Aisha, who said: When the people of Mecca sent ransoms for their captives, Zaynab, daughter of the Messenger of God ﷺ, sent a necklace belonging to her which Khadija had given her when she was conducted as a bride to Abu al-As. When the Messenger of God ﷺ saw it, he felt intense tenderness for her and said to the Muslims, “If you see fit to release her captive for her and return her necklace to her,” (1) and they did so.

(1) Transmitted by Abu Dawud in al-Sunan, 2/69, Book of Jihad, chapter “Concerning the Ransom of a Captive,” hadith no. 2692; Ahmad in al-Musnad, 6/276; and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, 3/236, 324. He said, “This is a sound hadith according to Muslim’s criterion, although neither of the two transmitted it,” and al-Dhahabi concurred with him.

Ibn Ishaq gave his story at greater length than this: Abu al-As attended Badr with the polytheists and was captured among those who were captured. Zaynab ransomed him, and the Messenger of God ﷺ stipulated that he send her to Medina, which he did. He later came with a caravan belonging to Quraysh; the Muslims captured him and took what he had. Zaynab granted him protection, so he returned to Mecca, delivered the deposits to their owners, and then emigrated to Medina as a Muslim. The Prophet ﷺ restored his daughter to him. The two accounts can be reconciled.

Ibn Ishaq stated that the man who captured him on the day of Badr was Abd Allah ibn Jubayr ibn al-Numan. Al-Waqidi related that the man who captured him was Khirash ibn al-Simma. He said: His brother Amr ibn al-Rabi came with his ransom. Musa ibn Uqba stated that the man who captured him—meaning on the second occasion—was Abu Basir al-Thaqafi, together with the Muslims who were with him when they took up residence [218] on the coast and waylaid the merchants of Quraysh during the truce between al-Hudaybiyya and the Conquest.

Ibn al-Muqri stated in his Fawaid, through Ibrahim ibn Sad, from Salih ibn Kaysan—I reckon from al-Zuhri—who said: Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi was the man in whose case the grant of protection first arose, in connection with the Quraysh caravan whose members were with Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl and Abu Basir ibn Utba ibn Usayd. He was brought as a captive, and the Messenger of God ﷺ said, “Zaynab has granted Abu al-As protection regarding his wealth and merchandise.” He went out and delivered to them everything belonging to them. She had asked Abu al-As for permission to leave for Medina, and he had given her permission. He then departed for Syria. When she set out, Hisham ibn al-Aswad and those who followed him pursued her and returned her to her house. The Messenger of God ﷺ then sent someone to carry her to Medina. Abu al-As subsequently joined her in Medina shortly before the Conquest. He said: He traveled with Ali to Yemen, and Ali appointed him his deputy over Yemen when he returned. Abu al-As was then with Ali on the day allegiance was pledged to Abu Bakr.

Abu Ahmad al-Hakim related that he accepted Islam five months before al-Hudaybiyya and then returned to Mecca.

Ibn Sad added that he did not attend any campaign with the Prophet ﷺ.

Al-Bayhaqi transmitted with a strong chain from Abd Allah al-Bahiyy, from Zaynab, who said: I said to the Prophet ﷺ, “If Abu al-As is reckoned close, he is a cousin; and if he is reckoned remote, he is the father of my child. I have granted him protection.” He said: It was also related from al-Bahiyy that Zaynab said this—and that version is mursal.

Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and Ibn Majah transmitted, through Dawud ibn al-Husayn, from Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet ﷺ restored his daughter Zaynab to Abu al-As under the original marriage contract. (1) It appears to have been derived from the aforementioned story. Al-Tirmidhi said concerning the hadith of Ibn Abbas: “There is no fault in its chain, but its basis is not known.” He said: “I heard Abd ibn Humayd say: I heard Yazid ibn Harun say ...” He mentioned these two hadiths and said, “The hadith of Ibn Abbas has the better chain, while established practice follows the hadith of Amr ibn Shuayb.”

Al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah transmitted, through Hajjaj ibn Artaa, from Amr ibn Shuayb, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Prophet ﷺ restored Zaynab to Abu al-As with a new dower.

It is established in the two Sahihs, in the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhrama, that the Prophet ﷺ delivered an address in which he mentioned Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi and praised him for his conduct as a son-in-law. He said, “He spoke to me and told me the truth; he made me a promise and fulfilled it.”

Al-Waqidi said: The Messenger of God ﷺ used to say, “We never found fault with Abu al-As as a son-in-law.” (2)

It is stated in the two Sahihs that the Prophet ﷺ would pray while carrying Umama, the daughter of his daughter Zaynab by Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi.

Al-Hakim Abu Ahmad transmitted with a sound chain from Qatada that Ali married this Umama after the death of her maternal aunt Fatima.

Ibn Manda said: Ibn Abbas and Abd Allah ibn Amr transmitted reports from him.

Ibrahim ibn al-Mundhir said: Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi died during the caliphate of Abu Bakr, in Dhu al-Hijja of the year twelve after the Hijra. Ibn Sad and Ibn Ishaq likewise dated his death to that year, and stated that he appointed al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam as his executor. More than one other authority dated it likewise. Abu Ubayd departed anomalously from them and said that he died in the year thirteen. Stranger still is Ibn Manda’s statement that he was killed on the day of al-Yamama.

(1) Transmitted by Abu Dawud, 1/680, Book of Divorce, chapter “Until What Point Is His Wife Restored to Him If He Accepts Islam after Her?” hadith no. 2240.

(2) Transmitted by Ibn Sad in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, 8/21.

uncertainties.location: The proposed original name ياسم in Ibn Manda’s report
uncertainties.issue: The word is unvocalized and the author himself presents Yasir as a textual corruption of it; its precise vocalization is therefore uncertain.

uncertainties.location: The phrase مواخيا لرسول اللَّه before the prophetic mission
uncertainties.issue: It can denote a formal bond of brotherhood or, more loosely, a brotherlike friendship. A formal pre-Islamic pact of brotherhood is not otherwise explained in the passage.

uncertainties.location: Ibn al-Muqri’s report: الذي بدا فيه الجوار في ركب قريش الذين كانوا مع أبي جندل بن سهيل وأبي بصير بن عتبة بن أسيد
uncertainties.issue: The syntax and historical relationships are difficult: the text appears to associate the Quraysh caravan with Abu Jandal and Abu Basir, although the surrounding accounts associate them with those intercepting Quraysh’s caravans. The wording may be defective or compressed.
uncertainties.best_rendering: Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi was the man in whose case the grant of protection first arose, in connection with the Quraysh caravan whose members were with Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl and Abu Basir ibn Utba ibn Usayd

uncertainties.location: Zaynab’s statement إن قرب فابن عم، وإن بعد فأبو ولد
uncertainties.issue: أبو ولد is elliptical and literally means “father of a child”; in context it most likely means the father of Zaynab’s child.
